43.sec: Kshaharata inscriptions → issuer + content; Satavahana reconquest

43.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the two branches of the Western Kshatrapas?
o: Kshaharatas—Western Deccan; Kardamakas—Ujjain, Malwa and Kathiawar
Kshaharatas—Ujjain and Malwa; Kardamakas—Nasik and Junnar
43.x: The Kshaharatas were associated with the Western Deccan, whereas the Kardamakas ruled around Ujjain, Malwa and Kathiawar.
43.tq: Compare the branches by territory rather than by ruler alone.
43.sec: Western Kshatrapas - Kshaharatas vs Kardamakas; coinage metals

43.s: Which of the following rulers belonged to the Kardamaka branch?
43.x: Chashtana belonged to the Kardamaka branch. Bhumaka and Nahapana belonged to the Kshaharata branch.
43.tq: Use ruler–branch discrimination among closely related names.
43.sec: Western Kshatrapas - Kshaharatas vs Kardamakas; coinage metals

43.s: The clash between Chashtana and Vasishthiputra Pulumavi is referred to by which ancient writer?
43.x: Ptolemy records the clash between Chashtana and the Satavahana ruler Vasishthiputra Pulumavi.
43.tq: Match the historical event with the relevant classical source.
43.sec: Western Kshatrapas - Kshaharatas vs Kardamakas; coinage metals

43.s: Which statement regarding the coinage of the Western Kshatrapas is correct?
o: Their principal coins were exclusively gold.
Their silver coins were numerous in western India, and Kardamaka coins carried Saka-era dates.
Their coins were issued only in copper and bore Gupta-era dates.
Their silver coins were confined to the eastern Deccan.
43.x: Numerous silver coins have been found in western India, and Kardamaka silver coins carried dates in the Saka era.
43.tq: Avoid absolute wording and combine metal, region and dating evidence.
43.sec: Western Kshatrapas - Kshaharatas vs Kardamakas; coinage metals

43.s: The gold-to-silver coin ratio referred to in the Nasik record is:
43.x: The recorded gold-to-silver ratio is 1:35, corresponding to one suvarna being equal to 35 karshapanas.
43.tq: Recall the exact ratio and distinguish it from the interest rate.
43.sec: Western Kshatrapas - Kshaharatas vs Kardamakas; coinage metals

43.s: The Sakas are described in the sources as ruling through which titles?
43.x: The Sakas ruled through the titles Satrapa and Mahasatrapa.
43.tq: Identify the characteristic administrative titles of a ruling group.
43.sec: Western Kshatrapas - Kshaharatas vs Kardamakas; coinage metals

43.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
43.x: Vikrama Samvat traditionally begins in 57 BC. The Kali Era begins in 3102 BC, the Saka Era in 78 CE and the Gupta Era in 319–20 CE.
43.tq: Start with the sure era–date pair and eliminate shifted dates.
43.sec: Eras → starting year + founder; converting dates

43.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Kali Era — 3102 BC
2. Saka Era — 78 CE
3. Gupta Era — Chandragupta I
4. Vikrama Samvat — Kanishka
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
43.x: The Kali Era begins traditionally in 3102 BC, the Saka Era in 78 CE, and the Gupta Era is associated with Chandragupta I. Vikrama Samvat is traditionally associated with Vikramaditya, not Kanishka.
43.tq: Detect the swapped founder or association in an era table.
43.sec: Eras → starting year + founder; converting dates

43.s: The Saka Era is associated in different historical and examination traditions with which of the following figures?
43.x: The Saka Era is commonly associated with Kanishka, while the Salivahana tradition credits Gautamiputra Satakarni.
43.tq: Handle a historically varied attribution without confusing it with the era’s starting year.
43.sec: Eras → starting year + founder; converting dates

43.s: If a date is given as Saka year 125, its corresponding Common Era year would be:
43.x: The Common Era year is obtained by adding 78 to the Saka year: 125 + 78 = 203 CE.
43.tq: Apply the stated era-conversion formula.
43.sec: Eras → starting year + founder; converting dates

43.s: A date expressed as Vikrama Samvat 200 corresponds approximately to which year of the Common Era?
43.x: The Common Era equivalent is obtained by subtracting 57 from the Vikrama Samvat year: 200 − 57 = 143? Wait, under the stated conversion CE = Vikrama − 57, the correct value is 143 CE.
43.tq: Apply the conversion rule carefully and check the direction of subtraction.
43.sec: Eras → starting year + founder; converting dates

43.s: Rudradaman I ruled approximately during which period?
43.x: Rudradaman I is generally assigned a reign of approximately 130–150 CE from Ujjain.
43.tq: Distinguish the ruler’s approximate reign from the era’s starting date.

43.s: The Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman I is significant because it is:
o: The first copper-plate charter of the Guptas
The earliest inscription entirely in Tamil
The first long inscription in Sanskrit
43.x: The Junagadh or Girnar record is regarded as the first long inscription in Sanskrit; earlier long records were generally in Prakrit.
43.tq: Identify historical significance through a distinctive superlative.

43.s: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I is dated to which Saka year and its corresponding Common Era year?
43.x: The inscription is dated Saka 72, equivalent to 150 CE.
43.tq: Link an inscriptional date with its era conversion.

43.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.
List-I
(a) Pushyagupta
(b) Tushaspha
(c) Rudradaman I
(d) Chakrapalita
List-II
(i) Repaired Sudarshana lake during the Gupta period
(ii) Built Sudarshana lake
(iii) Added canals under Ashoka
(iv) Repaired Sudarshana lake through Suvishakha
43.x: Pushyagupta built the lake, Tushaspha added canals under Ashoka, Rudradaman repaired it through Suvishakha, and Chakrapalita repaired it again during the Gupta period.
43.tq: Start from the sure pair and complete the sequence of repairs.

43.s: Who was Suvishakha in relation to Rudradaman I’s work on Sudarshana lake?
43.x: Suvishakha was Rudradaman I’s Pahlava minister, through whom the Sudarshana lake was repaired.
43.tq: Test the official’s identity rather than the ruler’s action alone.

43.s:
Which of the following statements about Rudradaman I and the Satavahanas is correct?
1. Rudradaman defeated Satakarni twice.
2. Satakarni was described as lord of Dakshinapatha.
3. Rudradaman spared Satakarni because of a close relationship.
4. Rudradaman’s daughter married Vasishthiputra Satakarni.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
43.x: All four statements are correct. Rudradaman defeated Satakarni twice but spared him because of their close relationship, and Rudradaman’s daughter married Vasishthiputra Satakarni.
43.tq: Verify a connected set of dynastic and military relationships.

43.s: Rudradaman I’s Junagadh record also mentions his conquest of which group?
43.x: The Junagadh inscription records Rudradaman’s conquest of the Yaudheyas.
43.tq: Recall the additional conquest attached to a major inscription.

43.s: The national calendar based on the Saka Era was adopted with effect from:
43.x: The Saka-based national calendar was adopted from 22 March 1957.
43.tq: Distinguish the adoption date from the calendar’s annual dates.
43.sec: Saka era as the national calendar

43.s: In a leap year, 1 Chaitra of the Indian National Calendar falls on:
43.x: In a leap year, 1 Chaitra falls on 21 March; in a normal year it falls on 22 March.
43.tq: Separate the normal-year and leap-year calendar dates.
43.sec: Saka era as the national calendar

43.s:
Arrange the following foreign groups in chronological order of their major appearance in ancient India:
A. Kushanas
B. Indo-Greeks
C. Parthians
D. Sakas
43.x: The sequence is Indo-Greeks, Sakas, Parthians and Kushanas.
43.tq: Fix the earliest and latest groups first, then place the middle two.

43.s: The first prominent Saka king in the Indian context is generally identified as:
43.x: Maues, also known as Moga, is regarded as the first prominent Saka king, around 80 BC.
43.tq: Distinguish the earliest ruler from later regional Saka rulers.

43.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
43.x: Rajuvula and Sodasa belonged to the Mathura branch. The Upper Deccan branch was associated with the Kshaharatas Bhumaka and Nahapana.
43.tq: Find the swapped ruler–region pair.

43.s: Which of the following was a centre of Saka rule?
43.x: Mathura, Ujjain and Girnar were important centres of Saka rule.
43.tq: Identify a regional centre from a restricted historical list.

43.s: The Sakas were frequently engaged in conflict with which ruling power in the Deccan?
43.x: The Sakas were often at war with the Satavahanas, especially in western and upper Deccan regions.
43.tq: Test the major political rivalry of the period.

43.s: The greatest ruler of the Parthians in the Indian context was:
43.x: Gondophares is regarded as the greatest ruler among the Parthians or Pahlavas in India.
43.tq: Separate Parthian rulers from Saka and Kshatrapa rulers.

43.s: The Takht-i-Bahi inscription is associated with which Parthian ruler?
43.x: The Takht-i-Bahi inscription near Peshawar is associated with Gondophares.
43.tq: Match an inscription with the correct ruler and location context.

43.s: According to Christian tradition, who visited the court of Gondophares?
43.x: Christian tradition states that St Thomas visited the court of Gondophares.
43.tq: Recall the religious tradition linked with the ruler’s court.

43.s: Which of the following is NOT regarded as a contribution or feature associated with the Shakas, Parthians and Kushanas?
o: Development of long Sanskrit epigraphic records
43.x: Their military tradition is associated with improved cavalry, not exclusive reliance on elephants. Dated silver coins and Sanskrit epigraphy are also important features.
43.tq: Reject the absolute military claim that contradicts the recorded cavalry contribution.

43.s: Which of the following groups of institutions is specifically associated with artistic patronage by the Shakas, Parthians and Kushanas?
43.x: These foreign ruling groups patronised the artistic centres of Sanchi, Mathura and Gandhara.
43.tq: Identify the complete set of associated artistic centres.

43.s: Which set of articles of dress and military equipment was shared by the Shakas and Kushanas?
o: Kilts, bare feet, helmets and elephants
Trousers, long coats, helmets and boots
43.x: Trousers, long coats, helmets and boots were features shared by the Shakas and Kushanas, along with a stronger cavalry tradition.
43.tq: Recognise the distinctive foreign dress-and-military combination.

43.s: The satrap system introduced or maintained by these foreign ruling groups is best understood as a system of:
43.x: The satrap system was a form of provincial administration in which satraps governed territorial units.
43.tq: Translate an administrative term into its practical function.

43.s: The foreign ruling groups were absorbed into Indian society as which social category according to the cited tradition?
43.x: The Shakas, Parthians and related foreign groups were absorbed into society as Vratya Kshatriyas.
43.tq: Recall the social assimilation category associated with foreign rulers.

43.s: Which ruler of the Satavahanas defeated Nahapana of the Kshaharata dynasty and restruck the coins issued by him?
43.x: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated Nahapana, the Kshaharata ruler, and restruck his coins as an assertion of Satavahana power.
43.tq: Use the ruler–achievement association and distinguish the conqueror from the defeated ruler.

43.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Satavahana centres:
1. Pratishthana is identified with Paithan.
2. Amaravati was a Satavahana centre.
3. The Satavahana centre shifted to Amaravati after Rudradaman's defeat of Pulumavi.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
43.x: All three statements are correct. Pratishthana was Paithan, Amaravati was a Satavahana centre, and the centre shifted to Amaravati after Rudradaman defeated Pulumavi.
43.tq: Check each place-name and the cause-and-effect statement separately before selecting the coded combination.

43.s: Rudradaman I's defeat of Pulumavi is associated with which change in Satavahana political geography?
o: The transfer of the centre from Amaravati to Pratishthana
The transfer of the centre from Amaravati to Junagadh
The transfer of the centre from Paithan to Junagadh
The transfer of the centre from Pratishthana to Amaravati
43.x: Following Rudradaman I's defeat of Pulumavi, the Satavahana centre shifted from Pratishthana, or Paithan, to Amaravati.
43.tq: Apply the stated political event to identify the resulting geographical shift rather than merely recalling a place-name.

43.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Rudradaman I — Defeat of Gautamiputra Satakarni
Nahapana — Shift of the Satavahana centre to Amaravati
43.x: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated Nahapana. The shift to Amaravati followed Rudradaman I's defeat of Pulumavi, while the first long Sanskrit inscription was the Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I.
43.tq: Match each ruler with the event directly associated with him and reject swapped-person traps.

43.s: The Satavahana–Kshatrapa relationship included which of the following?
o: A treaty ending the use of coinage
A transfer of the Kshatrapa capital to Amaravati
43.x: The Satavahana–Kshatrapa relationship included a marriage alliance. The other alternatives are not associated with this relationship.
43.tq: Identify the precise form of inter-dynastic relationship and avoid replacing it with an unsupported political arrangement.

43.s: The first long Sanskrit inscription is generally identified with which of the following?
o: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I
The Nasik Prashasti of Gautamiputra Satakarni
43.x: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I is regarded as the first long Sanskrit inscription.
43.tq: Use the first-in-sequence clue and distinguish the inscription from other records associated with the same period.

43.s: The Nasik Prashasti is associated with which of the following rulers?
43.x: The Nasik Prashasti is associated with Gautamiputra Satakarni and forms part of the evidence used to recall his achievements.
43.tq: Link the inscriptional record to its ruler while avoiding confusion among contemporary Satavahana and Kshatrapa rulers.

44.s: Who among the following united the five Yuezhi clans and took control of the Kabul valley and Kashmir?
44.x: Kujula Kadphises, also known as Kadphises I, united the five Yuezhi clans and occupied the Kabul valley and Kashmir.
44.tq: Identify the ruler by linking the specific territorial and political achievement.

44.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Vima Taktu — Successor of Vasudeva I
Vima Kadphises — Extension of the empire to Mathura and Varanasi
Huvishka — Founder of the Kushana dynasty
Vasudeva I — Convenor of the Fourth Buddhist Council
44.x: Vima Kadphises extended Kushana authority to Mathura and Varanasi. The other rulers are associated with different stages of Kushana history.
44.tq: Use the ruler–achievement association and reject swapped deeds.

44.s: Vima Taktu occupied which position in the Kushana succession?
o: Between Kujula Kadphises and Vima Kadphises
44.x: The Rabatak genealogy places Vima Taktu between Kujula Kadphises and Vima Kadphises.
44.tq: Test succession order using the nearest neighbouring rulers as distractors.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about the Kushana rulers:
1. Kanishka is associated with the zenith of the Kushana Empire.
2. Huvishka was a successor of Kanishka and Mathura became a major centre during his reign.
3. Vasudeva I was the first ruler of the Kushana dynasty.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Kanishka represented the zenith of Kushana power, and Huvishka was his successor with Mathura as an important centre. Vasudeva I was the last great Kushan, not the first ruler.
44.tq: Find the incorrect dynastic-position statement before selecting the coded combination.

44.s: Vasudeva I is particularly noted for which of the following features?
o: Uniting the five Yuezhi clans and occupying Kashmir
Introducing the Saka era and convening the Fourth Buddhist Council
Being the founder of the Kushana dynasty and issuing copper coins only
Being the last great Kushan, bearing an Indian name and depicting Shiva on his coins
44.x: Vasudeva I was the last great Kushan, had an Indian name, and depicted Shiva on his coins.
44.tq: Distinguish the final major ruler from the founder, coin issuer and council patron.

44.s: The Kushanas were originally identified with which group?
o: Yueh-chi from north-west China and Central Asia
Scythians from western Europe and Egypt
Huns from the Deccan and Sri Lanka
Parthians from southern Iran and Mesopotamia
44.x: The Kushanas were a branch of the Yueh-chi who came from north-west China and Central Asia.
44.tq: Test the geographical origin of the ruling people against nearby foreign groups.

44.s:
The titles adopted by Kushana rulers reflected influences from which of the following regions or traditions?
1. Devaputra — China
2. Shaonano Shao — Persia
3. Kaisara — Rome
4. Maharaja — India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
44.x: Devaputra reflected Chinese influence, Shaonano Shao Persian influence, Kaisara the Roman Caesar tradition, and Maharaja the Indian tradition.
44.tq: Match each title with its cultural source before choosing the complete combination.

44.s: Which of the following military developments is associated with the Shakas and Kushanas?
o: Exclusive dependence on war elephants and chariots
Replacement of cavalry by naval forces
Improved cavalry and wider use of saddles and reins
44.x: The Shakas and Kushanas improved cavalry and promoted the wider use of saddles and reins in riding.
44.tq: Identify the practical military innovation rather than an extreme or reversed claim.
44.sec: Items introduced by Shakas and Kushanas  [other exams]

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched with the Fourth Buddhist Council?
44.x: Ajatasatru was associated with the First Buddhist Council. The Fourth Council was patronised by Kanishka at Kundalvana in Kashmir and used Sanskrit.
44.tq: Find the council-related person belonging to a different chronological event.

44.s: The Fourth Buddhist Council is generally dated to approximately:
44.x: The Fourth Buddhist Council is generally dated to approximately 72 CE.
44.tq: Distinguish the council date from the nearby Saka-era date and later Kushana dates.

44.s: Which one of the following was an outcome of the Fourth Buddhist Council?
44.x: The Mahavibhasha was compiled as an important outcome of the Fourth Buddhist Council. The council also dealt with disputes among Sarvastivada teachers.
44.tq: Associate the council with its distinctive textual outcome.

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Fourth Buddhist Council:
1. It formally marked the division between Mahayana and Hinayana.
2. It settled disputes among Sarvastivada teachers of Kashmir and Gandhara.
3. It was conducted in Sanskrit, whereas earlier councils used Pali or Prakrit.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All three statements are correct. The council formalised the Mahayana–Hinayana division, addressed Sarvastivada disputes, and used Sanskrit instead of the earlier Pali or Prakrit practice.
44.tq: Check whether all three statements describe distinct features of the same council.

44.s:
Arrange the following Buddhist Councils in chronological order:
A. Council at Pataliputra under Ashoka
B. Council at Kashmir under Kanishka
C. Council at Rajagriha under Ajatasatru
D. Council at Vaishali under Kalasoka
44.x: The correct sequence is the First Council at Rajagriha, the Second at Vaishali, the Third at Pataliputra and the Fourth at Kashmir.
44.tq: Fix the first and last councils, then place the Vaishali and Pataliputra councils between them.

44.s: The gold dinara of the Kushanas followed approximately which monetary standard and weight?
o: Roman weight standard, about 8 grams or 120 grains
Indian punch-marked standard, about 12 grams or 180 grains
Persian weight standard, about 4 grams or 60 grains
Greek weight standard, about 16 grams or 240 grains
44.x: The Kushana gold dinara followed the Roman weight standard and weighed approximately 8 grams, equivalent to 120 grains.
44.tq: Link the coin denomination with both its standard and approximate weight.
44.sec: Kushana coinage - FIRST large-scale gold, deities, portraits  [other exams]

44.s: Which of the following statements about Kushana coinage is correct?
o: Copper and lead coins were prohibited during the Kushana period.
Gold coins were of approximately 22–23 carat purity, while copper and lead coins were used extensively for daily trade.
Kushana gold coins followed a purely indigenous weight standard and contained less than 10 carat gold.
Kushana coins were exclusively silver and were never used in daily transactions.
44.x: Kushana gold coins were approximately 22–23 carat, while plentiful copper and lead coins circulated for daily trade.
44.tq: Compare precious-metal purity with the practical use of base-metal coins.
44.sec: Kushana coinage - FIRST large-scale gold, deities, portraits  [other exams]

44.s: Which of the following groups correctly represents the range of deities depicted on Kushana coins?
o: Greek, Iranian and Indian deities including Helios, Mithra and Shiva
Only Vedic deities such as Indra and Agni
Roman emperors and Egyptian pharaohs alone
Only Buddhist figures and Jain Tirthankaras
44.x: Kushana coins depicted more than thirty deities from Greek, Iranian and Indian traditions, including Helios, Mithra and Shiva.
44.tq: Use the religiously plural character of Kushana coinage to reject exclusive options.
44.sec: Kushana coinage - FIRST large-scale gold, deities, portraits  [other exams]

44.s: On the coins of Kanishka, the king is characteristically shown:
o: Seated under a Bodhi tree with a manuscript
Seated on a throne wearing a Roman toga
Standing in a peaked helmet, long coat and boots, sacrificing at an altar
Riding an elephant while holding a plough
44.x: Kanishka is shown standing in a peaked helmet, long coat and boots and making a sacrifice at an altar.
44.tq: Identify the ruler through the distinctive portrait details rather than the general coin type.
44.sec: Kushana coinage - FIRST large-scale gold, deities, portraits  [other exams]

44.s: Who wrote Buddhacharita, a Sanskrit account of the life of the Buddha?
44.x: Ashvaghosha of Pataliputra composed Buddhacharita in Sanskrit and was also vice-president of the Fourth Buddhist Council.
44.tq: Match the scholar with his best-known work while using other court scholars as distractors.

44.s: Which scholar is associated with Madhyamika philosophy and the work Suhrllekha?
44.x: Nagarjuna is associated with Madhyamika philosophy and Suhrllekha, a letter addressed to a Satavahana king.
44.tq: Discriminate among court scholars by their philosophical and literary contributions.

44.s: Who among the following was the court physician of Kanishka and the author of Charaka Samhita?
44.x: Charaka served as the court physician and is associated with the Charaka Samhita.
44.tq: Match the professional role with the corresponding scholar and text.

44.s:
Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the scholars associated with Kanishka's court?
1. Vasumitra presided over the Fourth Buddhist Council.
2. Parshva urged Kanishka to hold the Council.
3. Mathara appears in the court-scholar list.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
44.x: All three statements are correct. Vasumitra was president, Parshva encouraged Kanishka to convene the council, and Mathara is included in the court list.
44.tq: Verify each scholar through a separate role or association before choosing the combined answer.

44.s: What did I-tsing report about Nagarjuna's Suhrllekha?
o: It was prohibited in Indian monasteries.
It was written in Greek for Roman merchants.
It was used only as a royal tax register.
44.x: I-tsing recorded that he saw students in India memorising Nagarjuna's Suhrllekha.
44.tq: Test the precise observation of the foreign traveller rather than the authorship of the work.

44.s: Which city was the main or winter capital of Kanishka?
44.x: Purushapura, identified with Peshawar, was Kanishka's main or winter capital. Mathura was another capital, while Surkh Kotal was a provincial centre.
44.tq: Distinguish the principal capital from the second capital and provincial centre.
44.sec: Kanishka - capitals, extent, Rabatak, Sarnath, China  [other exams]

44.s: Which of the following correctly describes the territorial extent of Kanishka's empire?
o: Only the Kabul valley and Kashmir
From the Narmada to Sri Lanka, excluding north-western regions
From the Euphrates to the Nile, including Egypt
From the Oxus to the Ganga, including Kashgar, Khotan and Yarkand
44.x: Kanishka's empire extended from the Oxus to the Ganga and included Kashgar, Khotan and Yarkand in the Tarim Basin.
44.tq: Use the two boundary rivers and the named Tarim Basin cities to identify the correct extent.
44.sec: Kanishka - capitals, extent, Rabatak, Sarnath, China  [other exams]

44.s: Which of the following sequences represents the genealogy given in the Rabatak inscription?
o: Kujula Kadphises → Vima Taktu → Vima Kadphises → Kanishka
Vima Taktu → Kujula Kadphises → Kanishka → Vima Kadphises
Kanishka → Vima Kadphises → Vima Taktu → Kujula Kadphises
Kujula Kadphises → Kanishka → Huvishka → Vima Taktu
44.x: The Rabatak inscription gives the succession as Kujula Kadphises, Vima Taktu, Vima Kadphises and Kanishka.
44.tq: Arrange the rulers using the inscriptional genealogy rather than general dynastic prominence.
44.sec: Kanishka - capitals, extent, Rabatak, Sarnath, China  [other exams]

44.s: Which group of Indian cities is named in the Rabatak inscription as being under Kanishka?
o: Saketa, Kaushambi, Pataliputra, Sri-Champa and Ujjain
Pratishthana, Amaravati, Vatapi, Badami and Kalyani
Taxila, Madurai, Kanchipuram, Puhar and Vengi
Rajagriha, Vaishali, Nalanda, Kannauj and Thanesar
44.x: The Rabatak inscription names Saketa, Kaushambi, Pataliputra, Sri-Champa and Ujjain among the Indian cities under Kanishka.
44.tq: Recognise the inscriptional city-list as a fixed group rather than selecting a geographically mixed list.
44.sec: Kanishka - capitals, extent, Rabatak, Sarnath, China  [other exams]

44.s: The Sarnath image inscription records the dedication of a Bodhisattva image by:
o: Charaka in the tenth year of Vima Kadphises
Vasumitra in the fourth year of Vasudeva I
Friar Bala in the third year of Kanishka
Nagarjuna in the first year of Huvishka
44.x: The Sarnath inscription records that Friar Bala dedicated a Bodhisattva image in the third year of Kanishka.
44.tq: Combine the donor, object and regnal-year details to avoid swapped inscriptional facts.
44.sec: Kanishka - capitals, extent, Rabatak, Sarnath, China  [other exams]

44.s: The rise of Mahayana Buddhism after the Fourth Council was associated with which development?
o: Worship of Buddha through images and elevation of Buddha to the status of a god
Complete rejection of Sanskrit and exclusive use of Pali
Replacement of Buddhism by Jainism in Central Asia
Abandonment of all symbols and images
44.x: Mahayana followers made images of the Buddha and worshipped him as a god. Hinayana retained orthodox teaching and symbols.
44.tq: Apply the doctrinal distinction between image-centred Mahayana and orthodox Hinayana.
44.sec: Rise of Mahayana and Buddha-image worship  [other exams]

44.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the cultural transition associated with the Kushanas?
o: From Sanskrit Mahayana to Pali-Prakrit Hinayana
From Greek religion to Vedic ritualism alone
From Pali-Prakrit Hinayana to Sanskrit Mahayana
From Buddhism to exclusive worship of Shiva
44.x: The Kushanas helped move Buddhism from the Pali-Prakrit Hinayana tradition towards Sanskrit Mahayana.
44.tq: Test the direction of change by carefully separating the starting and ending traditions.
44.sec: Rise of Mahayana and Buddha-image worship  [other exams]

44.s:
Buddhism spread to which of the following regions during the period associated with the Kushanas?
1. Central Asia
2. China
3. Korea

46.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
46.x: ‘Trisamudradhipati’ is associated with Yajna Sri Satakarni, not Hala. Hala bore the title ‘Kavivatsala’.
46.tq: Find the swapped ruler-title pair among otherwise correctly matched titles.

46.s: Which one of the following titles was associated with Vasishthiputra Pulumavi?
46.x: Vasishthiputra Pulumavi bore the titles ‘Dakshinapatheshwara’ and ‘Navanagaraswami’.
46.tq: Separate Pulumavi’s titles from those of Satakarni I, Hala and Yajna Sri.

46.s: Which ruler is associated with the title ‘Trisamudradhipati’ in the tradition attributed to Banabhatta?
46.x: Yajna Sri Satakarni is associated with the title ‘Trisamudradhipati’ in the Banabhatta tradition.
46.tq: Use the title as a direct identification clue and distinguish it from ‘Trisamudra-toya-pita-vahana’.

46.s:
Arrange the following dynasties in the chronological order of their succession in Magadha:
A. Kanvas
B. Mauryas
C. Satavahanas
D. Sungas
46.x: The sequence is Mauryas, Sungas, Kanvas and then Satavahanas. Simuka is associated with the overthrow of the Kanvas.
46.tq: Fix the first and last dynasties, then arrange the intervening succession.

46.s:
Consider the following statements about the successors of the Satavahanas:
1. The Ikshvakus succeeded them in Andhra.
2. The Abhiras succeeded them in Maharashtra.
3. The Vakatakas succeeded them in Vidarbha.
4. The Pallavas were among their successors.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
46.x: The listed successors include the Ikshvakus in Andhra, Abhiras in Maharashtra, Vakatakas in Vidarbha and Pallavas. Chutus are also included among the successors.
46.tq: Treat each geographical succession as an independent statement before choosing the complete code.

46.s: Which of the following is the correct order of later political powers mentioned in connection with the succession after the Satavahanas?
46.x: After the Vakatakas and other immediate successors, the later sequence mentioned is Chalukyas followed by Rashtrakutas.
46.tq: Separate immediate successors from the later powers in the sequence.

46.s: Which of the following statements regarding Gautamiputra Satakarni is correct?
o: He defeated Nahapana and recovered territories including Malwa, Saurashtra, Konkan and Nasik.
He was the last great ruler of the Satavahana dynasty.
He belonged to the Kshaharata branch of the Western Kshatrapas.
He founded the Kshaharata branch and issued the earliest Nasik inscription.
46.x: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated Nahapana and recovered Malwa, Saurashtra, Konkan and Nasik. Nahapana belonged to the Kshaharata branch of the Western Kshatrapas.
46.tq: Apply the ruler–enemy–territory relationship and reject swapped identities.
46.sec: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Sri Yajna Satakarni  [APPSC]

46.s: Nahapana, defeated by Gautamiputra Satakarni, belonged to which branch?
o: Karddamaka branch of the Western Kshatrapas
Satavahana branch of the Andhra rulers
Kshaharata branch of the Western Kshatrapas
Chutu branch of the Deccan rulers
46.x: Nahapana was a Western Kshatrapa of the Kshaharata branch.
46.tq: Discriminate between the two branches by linking Nahapana specifically with Kshaharata.
46.sec: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Sri Yajna Satakarni  [APPSC]

46.s: The restriking of whose silver coins by Gautamiputra Satakarni is evidenced by the Jogalthambi hoard?
46.x: The Jogalthambi hoard contains Nahapana’s silver coins restruck by Gautamiputra Satakarni, providing evidence of Gautamiputra’s victory.
46.tq: Use the hoard as archaeological evidence for the ruler defeated and the victor’s action.
46.sec: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Sri Yajna Satakarni  [APPSC]

46.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
46.x: Ushavadata, also known as Rishabhadatta, was the son-in-law of Nahapana. Ayama was Nahapana’s minister.
46.tq: Watch for the APPSC person-and-role swap between Ushavadata and Ayama.
46.sec: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Sri Yajna Satakarni  [APPSC]

46.s: Ushavadata invested 2,000 karshapanas in which institution at Govardhana?
46.x: Ushavadata invested 2,000 karshapanas in a weavers’ guild at Govardhana.
46.tq: Link the precise amount with the economic institution rather than the donor’s family relationship.
46.sec: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Sri Yajna Satakarni  [APPSC]

46.s: Which ruler is associated with ship-motif coins and the extension of Satavahana rule into coastal Andhra?
46.x: Vasishthiputra Pulumavi issued ship-motif coins and extended Satavahana rule into coastal Andhra.
46.tq: Connect the coin motif with the ruler’s maritime and coastal expansion.
46.sec: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Sri Yajna Satakarni  [APPSC]

46.s:
Which of the following is associated with Yajna Sri Satakarni?
1. Revival of maritime power
2. Ship coins
3. Patronage of Nagarjuna
4. Association with the Nagarjunakonda Mahavihara
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
46.x: Yajna Sri Satakarni is associated with the revival of maritime power, ship coins, patronage of Nagarjuna and the Nagarjunakonda Mahavihara.
46.tq: Recognise the cluster of maritime, religious and architectural associations of one ruler.
46.sec: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Sri Yajna Satakarni  [APPSC]

46.s: The Periplus refers to which aspect of the history of the Satavahanas?
o: The Kanva conquest of the Deccan
The foundation of the Nagarjunakonda Mahavihara
46.x: The Periplus notes the conflict between the Sakas and the Satavahanas.
46.tq: Match the literary source with the specific historical relationship it records.
46.sec: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Sri Yajna Satakarni  [APPSC]

46.s: Which of the following literary works is NOT included among the traditions concerning the origins of the Satavahanas?
46.x: The Gathasaptasati does not narrate the early history of the Satavahanas. Traditions on their origins occur in the Kathasaritsagara, Dvatrimsatputtalika and Pratishthanapura Kalpa, among others.
46.tq: Find the work specifically excluded from the origin traditions.

46.s: Who wrote the Brihatkatha, which is mentioned in connection with Satavahana literary traditions?
46.x: The Brihatkatha is attributed to Gunadhya and was written in Paisachi.
46.tq: Match the literary work with its author and avoid confusing it with later retellings.

46.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
46.x: Katantra is associated with Sharvavarman and Kundala Satakarni. Leelavati Parinayam is associated with Kutuhala, while Brihatkatha is associated with Gunadhya.
46.tq: Use the three-part literary association—work, author and Satavahana connection—to eliminate swaps.

46.s:
Which of the following statements about the literary traditions of Satavahana origins is correct?
1. Somadeva is associated with the Kathasaritsagara.
2. Jain traditions and the Dipavamsa also contain traditions relating to Satavahana origins.
3. The Gathasaptasati is the principal source for the early history of the dynasty.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
46.x: Somadeva is associated with the Kathasaritsagara, and Jain and Dipavamsa traditions also discuss the origins. The Gathasaptasati does not narrate the early Satavahana history.
46.tq: Identify the single false source claim and retain the two supported literary traditions.

46.s: Which of the following statements regarding the chronology of the Satavahanas is correct?
o: The chronology contains no difference between Puranic and modern scholarly placements.
The dynasty is universally placed only between the fourth and fifth centuries CE.
The Puranic long chronology places Simuka approximately in 230–207 BCE.
The Puranic chronology places Simuka exclusively in the second century CE.
46.x: The Puranic long chronology places Simuka approximately in 230–207 BCE, while another chronology places the dynasty broadly from the first century BCE to the third century CE.
46.tq: Compare the two chronological frameworks instead of treating one disputed date as universal.

46.s: The chronology that places the Satavahana dynasty broadly between the first century BCE and the third century CE is associated in the material with which designation?
46.x: The CDI chronology places the Satavahana dynasty broadly in the period from the first century BCE to the third century CE.
46.tq: Distinguish a chronological designation from literary and travel sources.

46.s: Which ruler is associated with the Ashvamedha sacrifice, expansion into Central India and the issue of the first silver coins among the rulers listed?
46.x: Satakarni I is associated with the Ashvamedha, expansion into Central India and the first silver coins among the listed Satavahana rulers.
46.tq: Combine three distinctive achievements to identify the correct early ruler.

46.s: Satakarni I was a contemporary of which ruler?
46.x: Satakarni I is identified as a contemporary of Kharavela.
46.tq: Match the ruler to the contemporary from the same broad historical period.

46.s:
Which of the following statements about the Nasik Prasasti is correct?
1. It was composed in Prakrit prose.
2. It was written in the Brahmi script.
3. It records the expeditions, victories, empire and titles of Gautamiputra Satakarni.
4. It praises him as the destroyer of Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
46.x: The Nasik Prasasti is in Prakrit prose and Brahmi script and records Gautamiputra’s expeditions, victories, empire and titles, including his destruction of Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas.
46.tq: Treat language, script, contents and titulature as four separate inscriptional clues.
46.sec: Nasik Prasasti - issuer, reign, language, titles  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s: The Nasik Prasasti records gifts made by Gautami Balasri together with her son to monks on which hill?
46.x: The Nasik Prasasti records gifts made by Gautami Balasri and her son to monks on the Trirashmi hill.
46.tq: Identify the specific religious site linked with the recorded donation.
46.sec: Nasik Prasasti - issuer, reign, language, titles  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s: In the Nasik Prasasti, Gautami Balasri is described as the wife of a:
46.x: Gautami Balasri is described in the Nasik Prasasti as the wife of a Rajarshi.
46.tq: Recall the precise honorific relationship used for the issuer’s status.
46.sec: Nasik Prasasti - issuer, reign, language, titles  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s: Which of the following correctly identifies Vasishthiputra Pulumavi in relation to the Satavahana sequence and inscriptions?
o: He was the twenty-fourth ruler and is associated with the Amaravati inscription.
He was the sixth ruler and commissioned the Sanchi torana.
He was the twenty-seventh ruler and issued the first Nasik inscription.
He was the thirtieth ruler and ended the Satavahana dynasty.
46.x: Vasishthiputra Pulumavi is placed as the twenty-fourth ruler and is associated with the Amaravati inscription. The twenty-seventh and thirtieth positions belong to Yajna Sri Satakarni and Pulomavi III respectively.
46.tq: Combine dynastic position with inscriptional association to avoid ruler-number swaps.

46.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Yajna Sri Satakarni — patronage of Nagarjuna
Vasishthiputra Satakarni — marriage with Rudradaman’s daughter
Pulumavi III — revival of maritime power through ship coins
46.x: Pulumavi III is identified as the last ruler in the Puranic sequence, whereas revival of maritime power and ship coins are associated with Yajna Sri Satakarni.
46.tq: Find the contribution shifted from the last ruler to the last great ruler.

46.s: Which inscription is primarily associated with the military victories of Gautamiputra Satakarni?
46.x: The Nasik inscription records the military achievements of Gautamiputra Satakarni. Naneghat is associated with Satakarni I and Naganika, while Junnar and Karle contain Kshaharata records.
46.tq: Use the site–ruler association and reject the nearby inscriptional distractors.
46.sec: Inscriptions on Gautamiputra's achievements - site  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s:
With reference to the inscriptions connected with the Satavahanas, consider the following statements:
1. Gautamiputra’s own Nasik grant re-granted to monks land formerly held by Ushavadata.
2. The Naneghat inscription is associated with Gautamiputra Satakarni.
3. Junnar and Karle contain Kshaharata records.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
46.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because the Naneghat inscription is associated with Satakarni I and Naganika, not Gautamiputra.
46.tq: Split the options by identifying the wrongly assigned ruler.
46.sec: Inscriptions on Gautamiputra's achievements - site  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s: The Nasik Prasasti presents Gautamiputra Satakarni as belonging to which varna?
46.x: Balasri’s account presents Gautamiputra’s line as Brahmana. The inscription also describes him as the crusher of Kshatriya pride.
46.tq: Test the apparent contradiction between social status and military achievement.
46.sec: Social and religious claims in the Nasik Prasasti  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s: Which one of the following claims is associated with the Nasik Prasasti regarding Gautamiputra Satakarni’s social policy?
o: He fostered Brahmin families and upheld varnashrama.
He abolished the varna system completely.
He prohibited donations to religious institutions.
He made Buddhism the exclusive state religion.
46.x: The Nasik Prasasti credits him with fostering Brahmin families, upholding varnashrama and stopping varna-sankara.
46.tq: Match the ruler’s social claims with the precise action attributed to him.
46.sec: Social and religious claims in the Nasik Prasasti  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the religious patronage attributed to Gautamiputra Satakarni:
1. A village near Trirashmi was gifted to monks.
2. One hundred nivartanas of his own land were donated.
3. The Sanchi toranas are credited to him in the historical tradition.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
46.x: All three statements are associated with Gautamiputra’s Buddhist patronage. The southern Sanchi torana is also specifically attributed in one account to Satakarni II.
46.tq: Check each separate item of religious patronage before selecting the comprehensive combination.
46.sec: Social and religious claims in the Nasik Prasasti  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
46.x: Anupa corresponded to the Narmada valley, with Mahishmati as its capital. Aparanta was North Konkan, Vidarbha was Berar and Avanti was West Malwa.
46.tq: Start with the sure regional identification and eliminate reversed modern equivalents.
46.sec: Territories conquered - regions named in the Nasik Prasasti  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s: Mahishmati was the capital of which territory mentioned in the Nasik Prasasti?
46.x: Anupa represented the Narmada valley and its capital was Mahishmati.
46.tq: Test the territory–capital relationship directly.
46.sec: Territories conquered - regions named in the Nasik Prasasti  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Region)
 a. Aparanta
 b. Vidarbha
 c. Akara
 d. Avanti

List-II (Modern area)
 i. Berar
 ii. North Konkan
 iii. East Malwa
 iv. West Malwa

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
46.x: Aparanta was North Konkan, Vidarbha was Berar, Akara was East Malwa and Avanti was West Malwa.
46.tq: Start from the distinctive pair Aparanta–North Konkan and complete the regional matching.
46.sec: Territories conquered - regions named in the Nasik Prasasti  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Asika or Asaka — Godavari valley and Paithan area
46.x: Mulaka was associated with the Godavari valley and Paithan area, along with Asika or Asaka. North Konkan corresponded to Aparanta.
46.tq: Find the wrongly relocated region among closely related territorial names.
46.sec: Territories conquered - regions named in the Nasik Prasasti  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

46.s: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman is dated approximately to which period?
46.x: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman is a Sanskrit inscription dated approximately to 150 CE.
46.tq: Use the middle chronological value after distinguishing BCE, era and CE dates.

46.s: What does the Junagadh inscription state about Rudradaman’s conflict with Satakarni?
o: Satakarni twice defeated Rudradaman and annexed Saurashtra.
Rudradaman twice defeated Satakarni but spared him because of close relationship.
Rudradaman entered into a treaty with Simuka without any battle.
Rudradaman defeated Satakarni once and executed him.
46.x: The inscription claims that Rudradaman twice defeated Satakarni, the lord of Dakshinapatha, but spared him because of a close relationship.
46.tq: Watch for the combined action sequence: twice defeated, yet spared.

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Ptolemy records clashes between Vasishthiputra Pulumavi and Chashtana.
2. The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman was composed in Sanskrit.
3. The inscription describes Satakarni as lord of Dakshinapatha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
46.x: All three statements are correct. Ptolemy records clashes with Chashtana, while the Sanskrit Junagadh inscription identifies Satakarni as lord of Dakshinapatha.
46.tq: Verify the source, language and political title separately.

46.s: Vasishthiputra Satakarni’s queen, according to the Kanheri evidence, was the daughter of:
46.x: The Kanheri evidence identifies Vasishthiputra Satakarni’s queen as the daughter of Rudradaman, indicating a close Satavahana-Kardamaka relationship.
46.tq: Use the marriage relationship to distinguish the two ruling houses.

46.s: Who among the following later recovered territory lost by the Satavahanas?
46.x: Yajnasri Satakarni later won back territory that had been lost by the Satavahanas.
46.tq: Separate the ruler who faced the loss from the ruler who recovered the territory.

46.s: Which one of the following statements about the Satavahana political centre is correct?
o: The capital shifted to Amaravati, and the eastward movement made the Krishna valley the dynasty’s centre.
The Satavahanas had no capital in the Krishna valley.
The capital permanently remained at Mahishmati.
The capital shifted from Amaravati to Junagadh under Rudradaman.
46.x: The Satavahana capital shifted to Amaravati, also identified with Dhanyakataka, and the eastward shift made the Krishna valley the dynasty’s centre.
46.tq: Track the direction of political movement rather than confusing conquered regions with capitals.

46.s: Which statement best expresses the historical significance of the Satavahana dynasty?
o: It was the first historical dynasty of the Deccan and linked northern and southern India.
It was confined exclusively to the western coast.
It was a purely religious institution without political authority.
It ruled only the Narmada valley and had no southern connections.
46.x: The Satavahanas are regarded as the first historical ruling dynasty of the Deccan and as a link between northern and southern India.
46.tq: Choose the option containing both elements of the dynasty’s significance.

46.s: Which of the following statements regarding women in the Satavahana polity is correct?
o: Queens were excluded from all public activity.
Queens were not mentioned in Satavahana inscriptions.
Queens could act only as religious mendicants.
Queens are associated with a public voice in the Satavahana period.
46.x: The Satavahana period is significant for the public voice associated with its queens, as reflected by figures such as Naganika and Gautami Balasri.
46.tq: Identify the positive institutional feature instead of an absolute exclusion statement.

46.s: Which inscription is associated with the first Telugu word ‘Nagabu’?
46.x: The Amaravati inscription is associated with the first Telugu word ‘Nagabu’.
46.tq: Link the linguistic milestone with its inscriptional site.

46.s: The earliest inscription associated with the Satavahana line is identified in which region?
46.x: The first inscription associated with the Satavahana line is identified as the Krishna inscription.
46.tq: Distinguish the earliest inscription from later achievement inscriptions.

46.s: Which of the following correctly states the Satavahana first-and-last ruler tradition?
o: Founder Simuka; last ruler Pulomavi III
Founder Gautamiputra Satakarni; last ruler Yajnasri Satakarni
Founder Rudradaman; last ruler Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
46.x: The tradition identifies Simuka as the founder and Pulomavi III as the last ruler.
46.tq: Pair the two end points of the ruling sequence without importing intermediate rulers.

46.s: The use of metronymics among Satavahana rulers is stated to have begun during the reign of:
46.x: The use of maternal or metronymic names is stated to have begun during the reign of Gautamiputra Satakarni.
46.tq: Distinguish the ruler connected with the institutional naming practice from the later rulers who used it.

46.s: Current chronological reconstructions place Simuka’s reign approximately in which period?
46.x: The chronology places Simuka approximately in the period c. 230–207 BCE.
46.tq: Compare the competing BCE and CE ranges and select the period attached to the founder.

46.s:
Consider the following statements about the Satavahana historical tradition:
1. Debate continues regarding whether the homeland was in Maharashtra, Andhra or Bellary.
2. The long and short chronologies remain unresolved.
3. The Nasik Prasasti is the principal source for the reign of Gautamiputra Satakarni.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
46.x: All three statements are correct. The Satavahana homeland and chronology remain debated, while the Nasik Prasasti is the main source for Gautamiputra’s reign.
46.tq: Combine geographical debate, chronological debate and source criticism in one verification set.

46.s: Why are the conquest claims of the Nasik Prasasti treated with caution by historians?
o: It was composed several centuries after the Satavahana dynasty ended.
It was written by a foreign enemy of the Satavahanas.
It is a family eulogy and may exaggerate the conquests.
It contains no reference to any ruler or territory.
46.x: The Nasik Prasasti is a family eulogy, so its claims of conquest may be exaggerated even though its evidence remains important.
46.tq: Apply source criticism by identifying the purpose and bias of the inscription.

46.s: Which statement correctly identifies the chronological problem connected with the Salivahana era?
o: The era is unrelated to any Satavahana chronology.
The era began in 230 BCE and exactly matches Simuka’s reign.
The era is dated to AD 78, but attributing it to Gautamiputra does not fit his c. 106–130 CE dates.
The era began in AD 150 and exactly matches Rudradaman’s inscription.
46.x: Gautamiputra is credited in the tradition with the Salivahana era of AD 78, but that attribution conflicts with the dates c. 106–130 CE assigned to his reign.
46.tq: Compare the era date with the ruler’s proposed reign instead of accepting a famous attribution automatically.

46.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman
B. Approximate reign of Simuka
C. Reign period assigned to Gautamiputra Satakarni
D. Later recovery of territory by Yajnasri Satakarni
46.x: Simuka is placed around c. 230–207 BCE, Gautamiputra around c. 106–130 CE, Rudradaman’s Junagadh inscription around 150 CE, and Yajnasri’s recovery occurred later.
46.tq: Fix the earliest BCE item first, then place the dated inscription before the later recovery.

46.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
46.x: The first Telugu word ‘Nagabu’ is associated with the Amaravati inscription, not Junagadh. Dhanyakataka was a Satavahana capital and Mahishmati was the capital of Anupa.
46.tq: Separate inscriptional language evidence from political and territorial associations.

47.s: Who among the following Satavahana rulers is associated with the authorship of Gathasaptasati (Sattasai)?
47.x: Gathasaptasati was composed under Hala, the seventeenth Satavahana king, who bore the title Kavivatsala.
47.tq: Use the ruler–work association and distinguish the literary ruler from other prominent Satavahana kings.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Gathasaptasati?
o: A Paisachi grammar written in the Kuntala Satakarni period
A collection of Buddhist verses composed in Brahmi script
An anthology of 700 Maharashtri Prakrit verses dealing mainly with love, rural life and nature
A Sanskrit treatise on Jain philosophy containing 700 chapters
47.x: Gathasaptasati, or Sattasai, is an anthology of 700 gathas in Maharashtri Prakrit, dealing chiefly with love, rural life and nature.
47.tq: Identify the work through its distinctive combination of number, language and subject matter.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s:
Consider the following statements about Gathasaptasati:
1. It is regarded as an important literary source for Satavahana society.
2. It is a reliable source for the political history of the early Satavahanas.
3. It contains descriptions of rural life and nature.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: Gathasaptasati is an important source for Satavahana social life and describes rural life and nature. It is not considered a source for early Satavahana political history.
47.tq: Find the excluded use of a source; the political-history statement reverses the source’s character.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s:
Which of the following women are associated with contributions to Gathasaptasati?
1. Anulakshmi
2. Anupalabdha
3. Reva
4. Madhavi
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
47.x: Anulakshmi, Anupalabdha, Reva or Revati, and Madhavi are identified as women contributors to Gathasaptasati.
47.tq: Cover the complete membership of a named list rather than relying on one familiar name.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s: Which one of the following is NOT associated with the social picture presented in Gathasaptasati?
o: Compulsory military training for all women
47.x: Gathasaptasati refers to sati, the absence of child marriage and the plight of wives of seafaring merchants. It does not mention compulsory military training for all women.
47.tq: Locate the outsider by comparing each option with the social themes attributed to the text.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s:
Consider the following statements about the cultural information found in Gathasaptasati:
1. It refers to sugar and jaggery.
2. It mentions group dances and choral singing called Brundagana.
3. It provides evidence of house-wall paintings.
4. It refers to the hanging of criminals.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: All four features—sugar and jaggery, Brundagana, house-wall paintings and hanging of criminals—are included in the social picture associated with Gathasaptasati.
47.tq: Treat each social detail as an independent statement and select the complete combination.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s: Gathasaptasati opens with a prayer addressed to
47.x: The work opens with a prayer to Shiva.
47.tq: Test the opening invocation directly, using nearby religious figures as distractors.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s: Which of the following sets contains only early Telugu or Desi words associated with Gathasaptasati?
47.x: Atta, Addam, Potta and Pilla are among the early Telugu words associated with Gathasaptasati. Other recorded examples include Padi, Pandi, Ammi and Tuppu.

47.s: Which statement regarding Hala is correct?
o: He wrote Katantra grammar in Sanskrit during the reign of Kuntala Satakarni.

He honoured the poets Kumarila and Sripalita and his reign is regarded as a golden age of Prakrit.

47.s:
Consider the following statements about Satavahana-associated works:

47.s:
Brihatkatha served as the base for which of the following works?
1. Kathasaritsagara
2. Brihatkatha Manjari
3. Lilavati Parinayam
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
47.x: Brihatkatha formed the basis of Kathasaritsagara by Somadeva Suri and Brihatkatha Manjari by Kshemendra. Lilavati Parinayam is a separate work associated with Kutuhala.
47.tq: Separate derivative works from an unrelated literary title.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s: Lilavati Parinayam is associated with which of the following descriptions?
o: Nagarjuna’s commentary on Prajnaparamita at Amaravati
Hala’s marriage to the Sinhala princess Lilavati near the Bhimeswara temple at Saptagodavari
Sarvavarma’s composition of a Sanskrit primer at Paithan
Gunadhya’s translation of Brihatkatha into Sanskrit
47.x: Lilavati Parinayam by Kutuhala concerns Hala’s marriage to the Sinhala princess Lilavati near the Bhimeswara temple at Saptagodavari, identified with Draksharamam.
47.tq: Use the cluster of person, event and place to identify the correct literary association.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
47.x: Samayasara is a Jain philosophical work associated with Kundakundacharya. The other pairs combine unrelated authors, works or descriptions.
47.tq: Start with the complete three-part association of work, author and subject.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Suhrullekha and Ratnavali are associated with Acharya Nagarjuna.
2. Prajnaparamita is traditionally attributed to Acharya Nagarjuna.
3. Kamasutra and Nyayabhashya are associated with Vatsyayana.
4. Kathasaritsagara was written by Somadeva Suri.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: All four statements are correct. The listed works are associated respectively with Nagarjuna, Vatsyayana and Somadeva Suri as stated.
47.tq: Check several author–work associations together and avoid swapping neighbouring literary names.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s: Which of the following statements about Yogasara is correct?
o: It is associated with Kundakundacharya, though some references attribute it to Nagarjuna.
It is the source text of Kathasaritsagara written by Somadeva Suri.
It is the Sanskrit grammar of Sarvavarma.
It was exclusively written by Sarvasena in Maharashtri Prakrit.
47.x: Yogasara is associated with Kundakundacharya in the cited examination key, while some references attribute it to Nagarjuna.
47.tq: Handle a source-attribution variation without confusing it with the authors of neighbouring works.
47.sec: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors  [APPSC]

47.s: The most common metal used in Satavahana coins was
47.x: Lead was the most common metal used in Satavahana coins. Potin, copper, bronze and silver were also used.
47.tq: Identify the dominant item in a material-composition list, not merely an item that appears in it.
47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

47.s: Potin, used in Satavahana coinage, was an alloy of
47.x: Potin was a copper–tin–lead alloy used in Satavahana coinage.
47.tq: Test the exact composition of a technical term through element substitution traps.
47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

47.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Satavahana gold and silver currency:
1. The Satavahanas did not issue gold coins.
2. Roman gold coins circulated at places including Attirala, Salihundam and Vijayawada.
3. Silver coins were known as karshapanas.
4. Gold was used only as bullion according to the cited account.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: The Satavahanas issued no gold coins in the cited account, although Roman gold coins circulated. Silver coins were called karshapanas, and gold was used as bullion.
47.tq: Combine the distinction between locally issued coins, circulating foreign coins and bullion.

47.s: Which of the following places is NOT included among the locations where Roman gold coins circulated?
47.x: The listed locations include Attirala, Salihundam, Vijayawada, Vinukonda, Nagarjunakonda and Nellore. Kanchipuram is not included in that list.
47.tq: Test completeness of a geographical list by identifying the externally introduced location.
47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

47.s:
Ship-motif coins are associated with which of the following Satavahana rulers?
1. Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
2. Yajna Sri Satakarni
3. Gautamiputra Satakarni
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
47.x: Ship-motif coins are associated with Vasishthiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni. Gautamiputra Satakarni is associated with the beginning of portrait coins, not ship coins.
47.tq: Separate rulers by coin motif and reject the attractive but unrelated portrait-coin association.

47.s: The ship with an anchor motif on Satavahana coins is significant primarily because it indicates
o: the conquest of inland forest regions
47.x: The ship motif, including the ship with an anchor, is regarded as evidence of maritime trade.
47.tq: Infer the economic significance of a visual coin symbol rather than memorising the symbol alone.
47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

47.s: Which statement regarding the issue of ship-motif coins is correct?
o: Every later Satavahana ruler issued ship-motif coins.
No later Satavahana ruler issued ship-motif coins after the rulers associated with the motif.
Ship-motif coins were issued exclusively by the Shalankayanas.
Only Gautamiputra Satakarni issued ship-motif coins.
47.x: The cited account associates ship-motif coins with Vasishthiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni and states that no later ruler issued them.
47.tq: Watch for the extreme word “every” and distinguish the known issuers from later rulers.
47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

47.s: Portrait coins in the Satavahana period represent
o: a Gupta innovation copied by the Satavahanas
an indigenous innovation, beginning with Gautamiputra Satakarni
a Roman practice introduced only under Yajna Sri Satakarni
a practice restricted to copper coins of Hala
47.x: Portrait coins are regarded as an indigenous innovation, and their issue began with Gautamiputra Satakarni. Silver portrait coins became common after him.
47.tq: Link the innovation, initiator and subsequent development in one precise association.
47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

47.s: Gautamiputra Satakarni is especially associated with which development in Satavahana coinage?
o: Introduction of iron coins with copper coating
Replacement of Brahmi by Kharosthi legends
Exclusive issue of Roman gold coins
47.x: Portrait coins began with Gautamiputra Satakarni, while silver portrait coins became common after his reign.
47.tq: Distinguish the ruler linked with the beginning of portrait coinage from rulers linked with ship motifs.
47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

47.s: Bilingual silver portrait coins of later Satavahana rulers carried which languages on their two sides?
47.x: The bilingual silver portrait coins carried Prakrit on one side and a Dravidian language on the other.
47.tq: Distinguish languages from scripts: Brahmi is the script, whereas Prakrit and a Dravidian language are the linguistic forms.
47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

47.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Satavahana coin legends?
o: They were exclusively in Tamil written in Greek script.
They were in Paisachi written in Roman script.
They were generally in Prakrit written in Brahmi script.
They were exclusively in Sanskrit written in Kharosthi script.
47.x: Satavahana coin legends were generally in Prakrit and written in Brahmi script.
47.tq: Keep language and script separate while identifying the standard form of the legends.
47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

o: A silver coin was called a karshapana, while one suvarna was equal to 35 karshapanas.
A gold coin was called a karshapana and a silver coin a suvarna.
A silver coin was called a suvarna, while one karshapana was equal to 35 suvarnas.
Both suvarna and karshapana denoted only copper coins.

47.sec: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins  [APPSC]

47.s: Which one of the following was NOT a motif found on Satavahana coins?

47.s: The Ujjain symbol appearing on the reverse of Satavahana coins is represented by
o: a circle divided into eight segments

47.s: In the Satavahana administrative system, the term ‘Raja’ denoted which of the following?

The highest feudatory who could issue coins
A village assembly dealing with local administration
A minister responsible for royal revenue

o: Skandhavara was a city assembly, whereas Kataka denoted land revenue.
Kataka was a temporary campaign camp, whereas Skandhavara was a permanent garrison.
Kataka was a permanent military camp or fortified administrative centre, whereas Skandhavara was a temporary campaign camp.

47.s: Which of the following correctly describes the military organisation of the Satavahanas?
o: The army consisted only of infantry and cavalry, without elephants or archers.
The Chaturanga bala comprised chariots, elephants, cavalry and infantry, and archers also formed part of the military arrangement.
The king was not connected with military command, which was vested entirely in feudatories.
Archers were placed in front, while infantry was always stationed at the rear.
47.x: The Satavahana army was described as Chaturanga bala—chariots, elephants, cavalry and infantry—with archers also present. The king was the supreme commander.

Cavalry in front, infantry on the flanks, elephants at the rear
Elephants in front, archers on the flanks, cavalry at the rear
Archers in front, elephants at the rear, infantry on the flanks
47.x: Amaravati sculptures show infantry in front, cavalry and elephants on the flanks, and archers at the rear.

o: It was semi-feudal, and the king upheld the Dharmashastras.
It was completely centralised and had no feudatory elements.
It was a republican confederation governed by town assemblies.
It was governed exclusively by Buddhist monastic authorities.
